Downloading reports and extracting text

Source: vignettes/articles/downloading-reports.Rmd
downloading-reports.Rmd

Browsing the metadata needs nothing beyond the package itself. This article covers the next step: downloading the actual report files in bulk and turning them into analyzable text.

One-time setup: curl-impersonate

gao.gov’s servers reject requests from ordinary download tools, so the package uses curl-impersonate, a variant of curl that gao.gov accepts. Install it once:

# Arch Linux
sudo pacman -S curl-impersonate

# macOS
brew install lexiforest/curl-impersonate/curl-impersonate

For other platforms, prebuilt binaries are available from the curl-impersonate releases page. If the binary has a different name or location on your system, point the package at it with options(gao.curl_bin = "/path/to/curl_firefox147").

Everything else in the package works without it, and any function that needs it will remind you with these instructions.

Downloading reports

auto_download() is the one-stop function. Called with no arguments in an interactive session, it walks you through the choices — format, year range, and a confirmation with the total file count before anything is downloaded:

library(gao)

auto_download()

Or specify everything up front, for scripts:

# All reports from fiscal years 2023-2024, as PDF
auto_download(format = "pdf", year = 2023:2024, confirm = FALSE)

Files land in your working directory:

gao_reports/
├── pdf/
│   ├── gao-23-105043.pdf
│   ├── gao-23-105177.pdf
│   └── ...
└── html/        (with format = "html" or "both")

Downloads pause for one second between files (adjustable via sleep_time) to be polite to gao.gov. A full fiscal year is typically a few hundred reports, so plan for several minutes per year and a few hundred MB of disk space.

Metadata only, no downloads

format = "metadata" skips the downloads entirely and writes the filtered metadata to a CSV — useful when you only need the report list in a spreadsheet or another language:

auto_download(format = "metadata", year = 2020:2024, confirm = FALSE)

Extracting text

Once you have PDFs, extract_text() reads a whole directory into a data.frame — one row per file, with the full text of all pages in one string. It requires the pdftools package (install.packages("pdftools")).

texts <- extract_text("gao_reports/pdf")

nrow(texts)          # one row per PDF
texts$file[1]        # the filename
texts$pages[1]       # its page count
substr(texts$text[1], 1, 200)  # the first 200 characters of text

From here you are ready for standard text-analysis tools — for example, counting term mentions across reports:

mentions <- grepl("climate change", texts$text, ignore.case = TRUE)
sum(mentions)

Very old reports are scanned images rather than digital text; those yield NA text (with a warning listing the affected files), so filter with is.na(texts$text) before analysis.

Joining text back to metadata

Filenames follow the report URL slug, so you can connect extracted text back to the metadata in gao_links():

reports <- gao_links()
reports$file <- paste0(basename(reports$url), ".pdf")

full <- merge(texts, reports, by = "file")

Now every report’s text sits alongside its topics, agencies, requesters, and the rest of the metadata — ready for whatever question you are asking.
